title: Pteridophyta — Ferns and Allies
topicTitle: Pteridophyta: General introduction and characteristic features of pteridophytes; morphological structure and reproduction of Dryopteris; economic importance of pteridophytes
notes: **General features:** first vascular plants, have true roots, stems and leaves, reproduce by spores, dominant sporophyte, independent gametophyte (prothallus).

**Classes:** Psilopsida (most primitive, no true roots, e.g., Psilotum), Lycopsida (club mosses, microphylls, e.g., Selaginella), Sphenopsida (horsetails, e.g., Equisetum), Pteropsida (true ferns, megaphylls, e.g., Dryopteris, Pteris).
**Dryopteris structure:** large compound leaves (fronds), underground rhizome, adventitious roots, sori (clusters of sporangia) on leaf undersides protected by indusium.
**Reproduction:** homosporous (one type of spore). Spore germinates into heart-shaped prothallus (gametophyte) bearing antheridia and archegonia. Water required for sperm motility.
**Economic importance:** soil erosion control, ornamental plants (ferns in gardens), medicinal (Dryopteris used as anthelmintic), biofertilizer (Azolla with Anabaena in rice fields).
